title: U.S. households remain cautiously optimistic while inflation, generational affordability gaps, credit restraint, AI skepticism and fraud risk reshape financial behavior
source_unit: TransUnion Consumer Pulse Study, U.S. Q2 2026
geography: United States; adults aged 18 and older across all states

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed online by TransUnion and Dynata; quotas balanced to census demographics

income_increase.unit: percent saying income increased in Q2 2026, down from 30% a year earlier

income_stable.unit: percent saying income stayed the same, up from 53% a year earlier

inflation_top_concern.unit: percent naming inflation as a top household financial concern, up from 47% a year earlier

gas_concern.unit: percent very concerned about rising gas prices

observations.method: Online consumer survey with demographic quotas across age, gender, household income, race and region; reported margins are based on an unweighted panel and calculated error margin.
observations.uncertainty: This is a commercial cross-sectional survey of attitudes and self-reported plans, not administrative income or spending data; year-over-year comparisons may reflect sample, timing and wording effects.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with additional generational and income-level comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable or improving reported finances can coexist with greater concern because households may be responding to uncertainty, expected costs or salient gas prices rather than realized budget deterioration.

observations.period: Q2 2026; generational affordability and household outlook

denominator.unit: U.S. adults surveyed; generations defined by TransUnion as Gen Z 18–29, Millennials 30–45, Gen X 46–61 and Baby Boomers 62+

gen_x_finances_planned.unit: percent of Gen X saying household finances were as planned or better

gen_z_finances_planned.unit: percent of Gen Z saying household finances were as planned or better

gen_x_outlook.unit: percent of Gen X optimistic about household finances over the next 12 months

gen_z_outlook.unit: percent of Gen Z optimistic about household finances over the next 12 months

observations.method: Generational subgroup comparisons within the Q2 Consumer Pulse survey; the report also identifies Gen X as reporting every measured spending category as more unaffordable than other generations.
observations.uncertainty: Generational categories combine age with life stage, income, caregiving and debt exposure; subgroup differences are descriptive and do not isolate a generation effect.
observations.subgroup: Gen Z, Millennials, Gen X and Baby Boomers as defined by the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: Gen X’s squeeze may reflect the sandwich-care life stage and accumulated obligations, while younger generations’ optimism may reflect lower current obligations or different expectations rather than greater material security.

observations.period: Q2 2026; planned spending and credit behavior

discretionary_pullback.unit: percent of inflation-concerned consumers planning to cut discretionary spending in the next three months, versus 23% among others

credit_intent.unit: percent planning to apply for new or refinance existing credit, down from 33% in Q2 2025

inflation_concerned_credit.unit: percent of inflation-concerned consumers planning to seek new or refinance credit, versus 47% of others

interest_rate_refinance.value: Among interest-rate-concerned consumers planning credit, refinancing personal loans was 15% versus 9% among others, and home-equity refinancing was 14% versus 8%

observations.method: Survey of stated spending and credit intentions, with cross-tabulation by inflation and interest-rate concern.
observations.uncertainty: Intentions are not observed applications, approvals, refinancing or repayment outcomes; the source cannot establish whether credit restraint reflects prudence, exclusion, or both.
observations.subgroup: Inflation-concerned and interest-rate-concerned consumers, with generational and income comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower credit demand can signal healthier deleveraging or fewer borrowing opportunities; refinancing among interest-rate-concerned households may reduce rather than increase financial strain if completed successfully.

observations.period: Q2 2026; AI trust, fraud exposure and consumer protection

ai_positive_outlook.unit: percent believing AI will have a positive long-term impact on them, down from 39% in Q2 2025

ai_negative_outlook.unit: percent with a negative long-term AI outlook, up from 25% a year earlier

credit_monitoring.unit: percent monitoring credit at least monthly

fraud_targeted.unit: percent saying they were targeted by online, email, phone or text fraud in the prior three months

breach_action_gap.value: Less than half took protective action after notification of a data breach, and 17% closed the affected account

observations.method: Commercial consumer survey covering AI expectations, credit monitoring, fraud targeting, breaches and protective actions.
observations.uncertainty: Fraud exposure and protective actions are self-reported; the source does not independently verify incidents, distinguish severity or measure later identity-theft loss and recovery.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with younger consumers more likely to monitor credit monthly and older consumers more likely to cite fraud protection as a reason.
observations.counterinterpretation: Growing credit monitoring can indicate increased agency and financial vigilance, not only rising risk; low breach response may reflect notification fatigue, uncertainty or effective existing controls.

related_sources.claim: Official Consumer Pulse page with Q2 2026 findings, methodology and report library.
TransUnion consumer-credit context for affordability and credit-demand interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. household-resilience layer: aggregate optimism and financial stability coexist with generational affordability pressure, discretionary pullback, lower credit intent, AI skepticism, fraud exposure and uneven protective action. It is a TransUnion/Dynata online quota survey, not a longitudinal household panel, credit-bureau outcome dataset, verified fraud ledger, causal study or respondent-level financial trajectory.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official TransUnion Consumer Pulse Q2 2026 page was retrieved and reviewed for sample/methodology, income, inflation, gas, generational affordability, spending, credit intent, AI sentiment, credit monitoring, fraud exposure and breach-response findings; the site blocked direct shell download, so the hash is a canonical source-URL fingerprint rather than a downloaded-file hash.
